newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO ministers to meet new Russian counterpart.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers to meet new Russian counterpart.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov will receive a frank message from NATO on Thursday -- the Western Alliance is bent on enlargement but it wants to cooperate closely with Moscow, officials said.
Appointed little more than two months ago, Rodionov is to hold talks with the 16 NATO ministers at the end of a two-day informal meeting in the Norwegian west coast city of Bergen.

The NATO defence chiefs were discussing the expansion of the alliance as well as its command structure and a possible follow-on force for Bosnia, once the present 52,000-strong task force's mandate runs out in December.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said none of the 16 ministers had met Rodionov, whose government has expressed serious misgivings about NATO plans to take on some former Soviet bloc states as new members.
Since the end of the Cold War, ex-Communist countries such as Poland have been seeking to join NATO to guarantee their security against any future threat from Russia.
"The dialogue between NATO and Russia will be very intense. We will have an open dialogue, a frank dialogue," Solana said.

British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said it may be necessary in the talks with Rodionov "to underline to Russia that the decision for allowing NATO to grow in size has been taken. There is firm consensus on that subject".

A senior U.S. defence official earlier this week said Defence Secretary William Perry looked forward to private talks with Rodionov on continued cooperation -- following on from the close ties he developed with former Russian Defence Minister Pavel Grachev who was sacked in a government shakeup in July.
Perry has said he understands Russia's concerns about NATO expansion and that he strongly supports proposals for a new NATO charter giving Moscow a non-voting voice in alliance affairs.
NATO and Russia have developed a model for military cooperation in peacekeeping operations in Bosnia with the multinational Implementation Force (IFOR), said Portillo.

On Wednesday, the NATO ministers agreed they would probably have to keep thousands of troops in Bosnia next year. It was the first public acknowledgement by the alliance that such a force may be necessary to stop war from starting over again.
Officials said they had agreed to order the military to draw up options for a possible follow-on force. No binding decisions were taken in keeping with the meeting's informal character.
U.S. officials said Perry cautioned his fellow ministers against thrusting police duties on any new military force in Bosnia and said Washington was not anxious to send troops after war criminals.
French Defence Minister Charles Millon threatened to abandon plans for a full return into NATO in a row with Washington over who should head the southern region command in Europe.
The dispute, which surfaced on the margins of the Bergen meeting, could derail attempts to overhaul NATO's command structures and its plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
